# Italian glossary

**Generated from `glossary.json` — do not edit this file.**
Run `python .claude/skills/translate-it/scripts/glossary.py --md` after
changing the JSON.

One English term has exactly one Italian translation. Not a synonym, not a
near-miss, not "whatever reads better here" — the same word every time, in
the UI and in the data alike. A reader who meets *Stregone* on the character
sheet and *Incantatore* in a spell description has to work out whether the
app means the same thing. It does; the words should say so.

**STRICT** terms fail verification when they are missing from a translation.
**soft** terms only warn, because the English word is ordinary prose as often
as it is a game term (*a large room*, *reach the door*, *he will fall*).

## Never translated

- **dice** — 1d4, 2d6, d%, 1d4 x 10 — dice notation is universal
- **modifiers** — +2, -4, –2 — sign and number both, including the en dash the data uses
- **units** — the NUMBER never changes. The unit word may become Italian (feet -> piedi, pounds -> libbre) but must keep the same system: '10 feet' -> '10 piedi', NEVER '3 metri'. units.js converts at render and reads both languages.
- **markup** — every HTML tag, attribute and href exactly as-is: <p>, <i>, <a href="feats#power-attack">. Translate only the text between tags.
- **slugs** — anything that looks like an id: Link, ref, id, slug, anchors after #

## Adding a term

When a batch makes you choose an Italian word that is not here, add it to
`glossary.json` **in the same change as the translation that needed it**.
That is the whole mechanism by which the vocabulary stays consistent across
sessions, models and months: the first translator to meet a word decides it
once, writes it down, and everybody after that is bound by it.

Mark it `"strict": true` only if a synonym would be a real bug — a class, a
school, a save, an ability. Leave it soft when the English is also a common
word, or the checker will cry wolf on every other sentence.
